steps.why: This compares the two paths the textbook describes for sodium and identifies the easier one.

explain.title: Atoms form bonds to become more stable
explain.body: Atoms have a tendency to decrease their energy. They can do this by combining with other atoms. This is a natural phenomenon because it increases the stability of atoms.

explain.title: The duplet and octet rule
explain.body: The textbook says: “having two electrons (for hydrogen and helium which have only the first shell) or eight electrons in the outermost shell meant stability and hence unreactivity as well. This principle was named as Duplet or Octet Rule.”

explain.title: Atoms can take an easier path
explain.body: An atom may lose or gain electrons to complete a duplet or octet. The textbook’s example is sodium: it is easier for sodium to lose one electron than to gain seven.

explain.title: Hydrogen can gain or lose one electron
explain.body: The textbook explains that hydrogen can lose one electron to become H⁺ or gain one electron to become H⁻; gaining one electron completes its duplet.

mistakes: Saying sodium gains seven electrons instead of stating that it loses one electron along the energetically easier path.
Mixing up the duplet and octet: a duplet has 2 electrons, while an octet has 8.
Writing that all atoms must follow the octet rule; the section says later investigations found the rule less important.

modelAnswer: Atoms lose or gain electron(s) to acquire the electronic configuration of the nearest noble gas.

examTips: Board questions may ask you to define a bond or compare ionic, covalent and coordinate covalent bonding; give the defining electron process for each.
For sodium chloride, show the transfer equations Na → Na⁺ + e⁻ and e⁻ + Cl → Cl⁻, then state that electrostatic attraction holds the ions together.

hints: Ask whether electrons are transferred or shared.

yourTurn.question: How covalent bond is different from an ionic bond?
solution: A covalent bond is formed by the mutual sharing of an electron pair provided by the bonded atoms.
An ionic bond is formed by the complete transference of electron or electrons from one atom to another atom.
Final answer: A covalent bond forms by sharing an electron pair, while an ionic bond forms by complete electron transfer.
yourTurn.answer: A covalent bond forms by mutual sharing of an electron pair; an ionic bond forms by complete transfer of electron(s).

steps.why: Sodium has one electron in its outermost shell and loses it in the textbook's example.

steps.why: Chlorine gains the electron that sodium loses.
steps.text: e⁻ + Cl → Cl⁻

example.question: Explain the formation of sodium chloride from sodium and chlorine.
example.answer: Sodium transfers one electron to chlorine, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻; electrostatic attraction between the ions forms an ionic bond.

explain.title: What is a chemical bond?
explain.body: A chemical bond is a force of attraction between atoms which holds them together in the form of a molecule or a compound.

explain.title: Ionic bonds form by electron transfer
explain.body: An ionic bond is formed when atoms lose or gain electron(s) to acquire the electronic configuration of the nearest noble gas. The resulting oppositely charged ions are held together by electrostatic attraction.

explain.title: Covalent bonds form by sharing
explain.body: A covalent bond is a bond formed by the mutual sharing of an electron pair provided by the bonded atoms. One shared pair makes a single bond; two and three shared pairs make double and triple bonds.

explain.title: Coordinate covalent bonds have one donor
explain.body: Coordinate covalent bond is a type of covalent bond in which the shared electron pair is donated by one atom only. The donating species is the donor and the accepting species is the acceptor. An arrow points towards the acceptor.

explain.title: Polar and non-polar covalent bonds
explain.body: When a covalent bond is formed between two identical atoms, the shared pair lies midway between them and the bond is non-polar. Between non-identical atoms, the shared pair bends towards the more electronegative atom, making the bond polar.

mistakes: Do not describe an ionic bond as sharing electrons; it forms by complete transfer of electron(s).
Do not say that the whole ionic compound is one positive or negative ion; it contains oppositely charged ions.
Do not reverse the direction of a coordinate-bond arrow; it points towards the acceptor.
Do not confuse a double bond (=) with a triple bond (≡).
Do not say the two electrons in a coordinate shared pair come from different atoms; both are donated by one atom.
When explaining a polar covalent bond, state that the shared pair bends towards the more electronegative atom.

steps.why: Sodium is the comparison metal in the section's example, and its atoms release one electron each.
steps.text: In sodium metal, each sodium atom sets free only one electron.

example.question: Why does magnesium have a stronger metallic bond and a higher melting point than sodium?
example.answer: Magnesium releases two electrons per atom and acquires two positive charges, while sodium releases only one electron per atom. Magnesium therefore has a stronger metallic bond and melts at a higher temperature.

explain.title: The metallic bond
explain.body: A metallic bond, is therefore a type of chemical bond which has positively charged ions bound together by the mobile electrons. In a metal, the outer electrons move freely between spaces among atoms instead of staying attached to one particular nucleus.

explain.title: The strength of a metallic bond
explain.body: The strength of a metallic bond depends upon two factors: the number of positive charges present on the positive ions and the number of mobile electrons set free by each atom. Magnesium releases two electrons per atom, so its metallic bond is stronger than sodium's, where each atom sets free one electron.

explain.title: Conductivity
explain.body: The presence of freely moving electrons in metals makes them good conductor of heat and electricity. The mobile electrons can move through the metal.

explain.title: Hardness and changing shape
explain.body: In metals, the atoms are strongly held and arranged in the form of rows one above the other. This arrangement makes them hard and heavy. When pressure is applied, the upper rows of atoms slip pass the lower rows, changing the shape of the metal. Metals can therefore be drawn into wires and sheets.

mistakes: Do not say that the mobile electrons are attached to just one particular nucleus; the section describes them as moving freely among the atoms.
Do not confuse a metallic bond with an ionic bond: metallic bonding involves mobile electrons binding positive metal ions.
When comparing magnesium and sodium, include both the number of electrons released and the effect on bond strength.
For malleability and ductility, do not just write “metals bend”; explain that rows of atoms slip past one another under pressure.

explain.title: What electropositive character means
explain.body: Metals generally have a tendency to lose electrons to form positive ions called cations. This property is called the electropositive character of metals.

explain.title: Electropositive character and reactivity
explain.body: This property is also related to the reactivity of the metals. Metals which lose electron or electrons easily are considered more reactive.

explain.title: Alkali metals
explain.body: Alkali metals (Na, K) are highly electropositive elements and thus they undergo reactions very easily. Sodium and potassium react vigorously with water and halogens to give their respective hydroxides and halides. They also react with acids to give salts and hydrogen.

explain.title: Alkaline earth metals
explain.body: Alkaline earth metals (Mg, Ca), on the other hand, lose their outer electrons less easily and thus they are less electropositive than alkali metals. Their reactions towards water and halogens are also less vigorous.

explain.title: Aluminium
explain.body: Aluminum is also highly electropositive metal. It reacts readily with mineral acids to form salts and hydrogen.

example.question: Compare the properties of ionic and covalent compounds.
example.answer: Ionic compounds have oppositely charged ions arranged in a crystalline structure and usually have high melting and boiling points. They are generally soluble in polar solvents and conduct electricity when molten or in solution because they have free ions. Covalent compounds mostly exist as discrete neutral molecules, generally have lower melting and boiling points, are usually insoluble in water but soluble in non-polar solvents, and are usually bad conductors.

explain.title: Ionic compounds
explain.body: In ionic compounds oppositely charged ions are properly arranged to give a crystalline structure. As a whole the compound is neutral. There exists a strong electrostatic force between their ions. Ionic compounds are usually solids with high melting and boiling points. They are generally soluble in polar solvents like water and conduct electricity when molten or in solution because free ions are present.

explain.title: Covalent compounds
explain.body: Covalent compounds mostly exist as discrete neutral molecules. There exists a strong electrostatic attraction between the nuclei and the shared electrons. Lower molecular mass covalent compounds are gases or low-boiling liquids, while high molecular mass covalent compounds exist as solids. They generally have lower melting and boiling points, are usually insoluble in water but soluble in non-polar solvents, and are usually bad conductors of electricity.

explain.title: Use the particle explanation
explain.body: When explaining a property, connect it to the particles. For example, ionic compounds conduct electricity in the molten state or in solution because they contain free ions. Do not confuse this with solid ionic compounds, where the ions are held in the crystal arrangement.

mistakes: Saying ionic compounds conduct electricity as solids; the section says they conduct when molten or in solution.
Forgetting to explain that free ions are responsible for ionic conductivity.
Claiming that every covalent compound is a gas or liquid; high molecular mass covalent compounds can be solids.
Reversing the usual solubility patterns: ionic compounds are generally soluble in polar solvents, while covalent compounds are usually soluble in non-polar solvents.
Writing only one side of a comparison question instead of comparing both ionic and covalent compounds.

explain.title: What are intermolecular forces?
explain.body: The forces of attraction which are present between the molecules of elements and compounds are named as intermolecular forces of attraction. These attractive forces are generally very weak as compared to the bonding forces present between the atoms of substances. Among the three states of matter, these forces are the weakest among the molecules of the gases and the strongest among the molecules of solids.

explain.title: Why their strength matters
explain.body: Intermolecular forces affect physical properties. The stronger the forces among the molecules of a liquid, the higher its boiling point; stronger intermolecular forces also give a solid a higher melting point.

explain.title: Dipole-dipole forces
explain.body: These attractive forces are present between the molecules of a polar compound like HCl. In HCl, chlorine attracts the shared pair of electrons more strongly than hydrogen, making the bond polar. The partial charges cause HCl molecules to attract each other; these are dipole-dipole forces.

explain.title: Hydrogen bonding
explain.body: Hydrogen bonding is a special case of dipole-dipole attractive forces. When hydrogen is covalent bonded to highly electronegative elements like F, O or N then the large difference of electronegativity values will make the covalent bond highly polar. Strong dipole-dipole attractions are then observed among the molecules. Water molecules form hydrogen bonds, helping explain water's relatively high melting and boiling points.

explain.title: Ionic solids and their lattice
explain.body: Oppositely charged ions attract strongly and form a crystal lattice. The ions are held in fixed positions, so ionic compounds are stable solids with high melting points. If a force shifts the lattice, it can break, which is why ionic solids are brittle. Because the ions are spherical and can surround one another from all sides, ionic bonds are non-directional.

explain.title: Conductivity and hydration
explain.body: Solid ionic compounds do not conduct electricity because their ions cannot move. When molten, or dissolved in water, the ions can move and carry charge. During hydration, water molecules surround and interact with ions. In aqueous reactions, ions from different compounds can combine to form a new compound, sometimes as a precipitate.

explain.title: Covalent substances and their properties
explain.body: Many low molecular mass covalent substances have weak forces between their molecules, so they are gases or low-boiling liquids. In carbon solids, structure matters: diamond has a rigid network of strongly bonded carbon atoms, while graphite has layers that can slip past one another. Mobile electrons between graphite's layers let it conduct electricity.

explain.title: Water and molecular attractions

notes.title: Why atoms form bonds
notes.answer: Atoms form bonds to lower their energy and increase their stability.
notes.explanation: Atoms form bonds because combining can lower their energy and make them more stable. For example, sodium can lose one electron more easily than gain seven, while hydrogen can gain one electron to complete a duplet.
notes.simple: Atoms join with other atoms when doing so helps them become more stable.
examples: Sodium loses one electron rather than gaining seven to complete its octet.
Hydrogen can gain one electron to complete its duplet.
steps: Atoms can lower their energy by combining with other atoms.
A full outer shell is associated with stability: 2 electrons for a duplet or 8 for an octet.
Atoms may lose or gain electrons along an energetically easier path to reach this stable arrangement.

notes.title: How atoms form chemical bonds
notes.answer: Atoms form chemical bonds by transferring or sharing electrons, or by one atom donating a shared pair.
notes.explanation: A chemical bond is the force of attraction that holds atoms together. Atoms can form bonds by transferring electrons, sharing electrons, or sharing a pair of electrons donated by one atom.
notes.simple: Atoms stick together because they attract each other. They may transfer electrons or share them to make a bond.
examples: Sodium transfers one electron to chlorine, forming Na⁺ and Cl⁻; their attraction forms an ionic bond.
Two hydrogen atoms share an electron pair to form H—H, a single covalent bond.

notes.title: Metallic Bond
notes.answer: A metallic bond is a type of chemical bond in which positively charged ions are bound together by mobile electrons.
notes.explanation: In a metal, outer electrons move freely among positive ions. These mobile electrons bind the ions together and help explain the properties of metals.
notes.simple: Think of positive metal ions surrounded by a shared pool of moving electrons. The shared electrons hold the ions together.
examples: Sodium releases one electron per atom, so its metallic bond is weaker than magnesium's.
Mobile electrons in a metal help it conduct heat and electricity.
steps: Metal atoms can lose their outer electrons easily.
The outer electrons move freely between the metal atoms.
The metal atoms become positive ions.
The positive ions are bound together by the mobile electrons.

notes.title: Electropositive Character of Metals
notes.answer: Metals generally have a tendency to lose electrons to form positive ions called cations. This property is called the electropositive character of metals.
notes.explanation: Metals can lose electrons and become positive ions. How easily they lose electrons is linked to how reactive they are.
notes.simple: Electropositive metals give away electrons. Metals that give them away easily are more reactive.
examples: Sodium and potassium lose electrons easily, so they are highly electropositive and react vigorously.
Magnesium and calcium lose their outer electrons less easily, so they are less electropositive than sodium and potassium.
steps: A metal loses one or more electrons.
Losing electrons forms a positive ion called a cation.
A metal that loses electrons easily is more reactive.

notes.title: Electronegative character of non-metals
notes.answer: Non-metals tend to gain electrons and become negatively charged ions called anions.
notes.explanation: Non-metals have an affinity towards electrons. They tend to gain electrons and become negatively charged ions called anions. They are therefore, named as electronegative elements. Fluorine is the most electronegative element in the periodic table followed by oxygen, nitrogen and chlorine. Non-metals readily react with metals forming ionic bonds. Non-metals also combine with other non-metals to form a wide variety of molecular substances.
notes.simple: Non-metals tend to take in electrons. When they gain electrons, they become negatively charged ions called anions.
examples: A non-metal gaining electrons becomes a negatively charged ion called an anion.
A non-metal reacting with a metal forms an ionic bond.

notes.answer: Intermolecular forces are attractions between molecules. Dipole-dipole forces occur between polar molecules; hydrogen bonding is a strong special case involving hydrogen covalently bonded to F, O or N.

modelAnswer: In ionic bond formation, one atom transfers electron(s) to another atom.
The atoms become oppositely charged ions.
The electrostatic attraction between these ions forms an ionic bond.
In covalent bond formation, atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
The shared electron pair(s) form a covalent bond.

written.text: How do ions arrange themselve to form NaCl crystal.
modelAnswer: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions arrange themselves alternately in a regular three-dimensional lattice.
Each Na⁺ ion is surrounded by six Cl⁻ ions.
Each Cl⁻ ion is surrounded by six Na⁺ ions.
The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions holds the crystal together.

written.text: Explain the properties of metals keeping in view the nature of metallic bond.
modelAnswer: A metal consists of positive metal ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons.
The free electrons move through the metal and conduct electricity and heat.
The metallic bond is non-directional, so layers of ions can slide over one another while attraction is maintained.
Therefore, metals are malleable and ductile.
The strong attraction between positive ions and electrons also helps give metals high melting points.

written.text: Compare the properties of ionic and covalent compounds.
modelAnswer: Ionic compounds are usually hard crystalline solids with high melting and boiling points because of strong attraction between oppositely charged ions.
They conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water because their ions can move.
Many ionic compounds are soluble in water.
Covalent compounds usually have low melting and boiling points because the forces between their molecules are weak.
They generally do not conduct electricity and are usually not soluble in water.

written.text: The formula of AlCl₃ in vapour phase is Al₂Cl₆ which means it exists as a dimer. Explain the bonding between its two molecules?
modelAnswer: In AlCl₃, the aluminium atom is electron-deficient and has an incomplete octet.
A chlorine atom of one AlCl₃ molecule donates a lone pair to the aluminium atom of another molecule.
This forms a coordinate covalent bond between the two molecules.
The two chlorine atoms act as bridges between the aluminium atoms.
Thus, two AlCl₃ molecules form the dimer Al₂Cl₆.
